text: Kenneth Elton Kesey (/ˈkiːzi/; September 17, 1935 – November 10, 2001) was an American novelist, essayist, and countercultural figure who considered himself a link between the Beat Generation of the 1950s and the hippies of the 1960s. Born in La Junta, Colorado, to dairy farmers Geneva (née Smith) and Frederick A. Kesey, he moved to Springfield, Oregon, when he was 10 years old in 1946. Kesey was a champion wrestler in high school and college in the 174-pound (79 kg) weight division, nearly qualifying for the Olympic team before a serious shoulder injury ended his career; he graduated from Springfield High School in 1953. An avid reader and filmgoer, he admired John Wayne, Edgar Rice Burroughs, and Zane Grey, later naming a son Zane, and experimented with magic, ventriloquism, and hypnotism. While attending the University of Oregon School of Journalism and Communication in Eugene in 1956, he eloped with Norma "Faye" Haxby, whom he had met in seventh grade; according to Kesey, without Faye, he would have been swept overboard by notoriety and weird, dope-fueled ideas and flower-child girls with beamy eyes and bulbous breasts. They remained married until his death and had three children: Jed, Zane, and Shannon. With Faye's approval, Kesey fathered a daughter, Sunshine Kesey, with fellow Merry Prankster Carolyn "Mountain Girl" Adams, born in 1966 and raised by Adams and her stepfather, Jerry Garcia. Kesey had a football scholarship for his first year but switched to the University of Oregon wrestling team, posting a .885 winning percentage in the 1956–57 season and finishing second in his weight class at the Pacific Coast intercollegiate competition; he remains in the top 10 of Oregon Wrestling's all-time winning percentage. A member of Beta Theta Pi, he graduated in 1957 with a BA in speech and communication. Increasingly disengaged from playwriting and screenwriting, he took literature classes with James B. Hall, who introduced him to Ernest Hemingway and other literary modernists. After brief acting stints in Los Angeles, Kesey published his first short story ("First Sunday of September") in the Northwest Review and was selected for the Woodrow Wilson National Fellowship for the 1958–59 academic year. Unbeknownst to him, literary critic Leslie Fiedler influenced the committee to select Kesey alongside more traditional fellows. Because he lacked prerequisites for a traditional master's degree in English, Kesey enrolled in a non-degree program at Stanford University's Creative Writing Center. During his time there, he developed lifelong friendships with Ken Babbs, Larry McMurtry, Wendell Berry, Ed McClanahan, Gurney Norman, and Robert Stone. He frequently clashed with center director Wallace Stegner, who regarded him as "a sort of highly talented illiterate" and rejected his Stegner Fellowship applications, with Stegner's deputy Richard Scowcroft recalling that neither saw him as having a particularly important talent. Despite this, Kesey received the prestigious $2,000 Harper-Saxton Prize for his first novel in progress, Zoo, and audited a graduate writing seminar by falsely claiming his colleague had said he could attend classes for free. The course was initially taught by Malcolm Cowley, who was "always glad to see" Kesey and fellow auditor Tillie Olsen, and later by Frank O'Connor, whose frequent disagreements with Kesey led to his departure. While under Cowley's tutelage, Kesey began drafting a manuscript that evolved into One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. At the invitation of Vic Lovell, a Stanford psychology graduate student, Kesey volunteered to participate in a CIA-financed study under Project MKULTRA at the Menlo Park Veterans' Hospital, where he worked as a night aide. The project studied the effects of hallucinogens and other psychoactive drugs, including LSD, psilocybin, mescaline, cocaine, AMT, and DMT. Kesey wrote detailed accounts of his experiences with these drugs during the study and in subsequent private use. His role as a medical guinea pig and time at the Veterans' Administration hospital inspired One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. Published in 1962 under Cowley's guidance, the novel became an immediate commercial and critical success; in 1963, it was adapted into a stage play by Dale Wasserman, and in 1975, Miloš Forman directed a film adaptation that won the "Big Five" Academy Awards: Best Picture, Best Actor (Jack Nicholson), Best Actress (Louise Fletcher), Best Director (Forman), and Best Adapted Screenplay (Lawrence Hauben and Bo Goldman). Kesey originally participated in the film but left two weeks into production, claiming never to have seen it due to a dispute over the $20,000 he was paid for the film rights. He objected to the film not being narrated by Chief Bromden and to Jack Nicholson's casting as Randle McMurphy (he wanted Gene Hackman), though Faye Kesey said he was generally supportive of the film. In 1964, Kesey's second novel, Sometimes a Great Notion, was released, polarizing critics and readers; it is an epic account of an Oregon logging family's struggles and Kesey regarded it as his magnum opus. In 1965, after being arrested for marijuana possession and faking suicide, Kesey was imprisoned for five months. He fled to Mexico, returned to the U.S. eight months later, and was sentenced to six months at the San Mateo County jail on January 17, 1966. Two nights later, he was arrested again with Carolyn Adams while smoking marijuana on the rooftop of Stewart Brand's home in San Francisco. After his release, he moved back to the family farm in Pleasant Hill, Oregon, in the Willamette Valley, where he lived the rest of his life. He taught at the University of Oregon, culminating in Caverns (1989), a collaborative novel with his graduate workshop students under the pseudonym "O.U. Levon," and continued to contribute fiction and reportage to publications such as Esquire, Rolling Stone, Oui, Running, and The Whole Earth Catalog, with various pieces collected in Kesey's Garage Sale (1973) and Demon Box (1986). Between 1974 and 1980, he published six issues of Spit in the Ocean, a literary magazine featuring excerpts from an unfinished novel, Seven Prayers by Grandma Whittier, about his grandmother's struggle with Alzheimer's disease, and contributions from Margo St. James, Kate Millett, Stewart Brand, Saul-Paul Sirag, Jack Sarfatti, Paul Krassner, and William S. Burroughs. After the release of his third novel, Sailor Song, in 1992 to lukewarm reviews, he reunited with the Merry Pranksters and began publishing works on the Internet until ill health, including a stroke, curtailed his activities. In 1965, the Merry Pranksters, including Kesey, Neal Cassady, and others, took a cross-country trip in a school bus nicknamed Furthur, attempting to create art from everyday life and experience roadway America while high on LSD. This trip, described in Tom Wolfe's The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test and Kesey's unproduced screenplay The Furthur Inquiry, was documented with 16 mm film footage that remained largely unseen until the 2011 film Magic Trip. After the trip, the Pranksters held parties called Acid Tests around the San Francisco Bay Area from 1965 to 1966, many of which were hosted at Kesey's residence in La Honda. In New York, Cassady introduced Kesey to Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg, who introduced him to Timothy Leary. Sometimes a Great Notion inspired a 1970 film starring and directed by Paul Newman, which was nominated for two Academy Awards and in 1972 became the first film shown by the new television network HBO in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania. On January 23, 1984, Kesey's 20-year-old son Jed, a wrestler for the University of Oregon, suffered severe head injuries when the team's loaned van crashed after sliding off an icy highway on the way to Pullman, Washington; he was declared brain dead two days later at Deaconess Hospital in Spokane, and his parents gave permission for organ donation. Jed's death deeply affected Kesey, who later called him a victim of policies that had starved the team of funding and wrote to Senator Mark Hatfield criticizing the allocation of defense funds to national defense instead of addressing issues like cancer, heart disease, and highway deaths. At a Grateful Dead concert soon after promoter Bill Graham's death, Kesey delivered a eulogy, mentioning Graham had donated $1,000 toward a memorial to Jed atop Mount Pisgah. In 1988, Kesey donated $33,395 to purchase a proper bus for the school's wrestling team. Kesey was diagnosed with diabetes in 1992. In 1994, he toured with the Merry Pranksters performing a musical play he wrote about the millennium, Twister: A Ritual Reality, which took them from Seattle's Bumbershoot to Boulder, Colorado, including a sold-out two-night run at The Fillmore in San Francisco, where they coaxed Allen Ginsberg into performing with them. He mainly stayed in his home life in Pleasant Hill, preferring to make artistic contributions online or hold ritualistic revivals in the spirit of the Acid Test. In the Grateful Dead DVD The Closing of Winterland (2003), documenting the New Year's 1978/1979 concert at the Winterland Arena in San Francisco, Kesey is featured in a between-set interview. On August 14, 1997, Kesey and the Pranksters attended a Phish concert in Darien Lake, New York, and appeared onstage with the band, performing a dance-trance-jam session involving several characters from the group's mythology.

In 1994, Kesey toured with members of the Merry Pranksters, performing a musical play he wrote about the millennium titled Twister: A Ritual Reality. Many old and new friends and family supported the Pranksters on this tour, which began at Seattle's Bumbershoot and traveled along the West Coast, including a sold-out two-night run at The Fillmore in San Francisco and a stop in Boulder, Colorado, where they persuaded the Beat Generation poet Allen Ginsberg to perform with them. Kesey primarily remained in his home life in Pleasant Hill, focusing on artistic contributions through the Internet or organizing ritualistic revivals in the spirit of the Acid Test. In the Grateful Dead DVD The Closing of Winterland (2003), which documents the New Year's 1978/1979 concert at the Winterland Arena in San Francisco, Kesey is featured in a between-set interview. On August 14, 1997, Kesey and the Pranksters attended a Phish concert in Darien Lake, New York, where they appeared onstage and performed a dance-trance-jam session featuring characters from The Wizard of Oz and Frankenstein. In June 2001, Kesey delivered the keynote speech at The Evergreen State College's commencement ceremony. His last major work was an essay for Rolling Stone magazine advocating for peace in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks. In 1997, health issues began affecting Kesey, beginning with a stroke. On October 25, 2001, he underwent surgery at Sacred Heart Medical Center in Eugene to remove a liver tumor; he did not recover and died of complications several weeks later on November 10 at age 66. After a public service in Eugene, his body was returned to his farm and buried next to his son Jed. The film Gerry (2002) is dedicated to Kesey, and in the 2025 film The Chronology of Water, Kesey is portrayed by Jim Belushi. Kesey Square is located in downtown Eugene, Oregon.
